docs.title: A/B testing
docs.text: Random assignment creates comparable groups; a shared metric defines what is compared. A p-value describes how surprising the data would be under a specified null hypothesis. It is not the probability that the hypothesis is true. Decide the measurement and testing plan before interpreting a favourable result. Before launch, write down: - Unit of randomization - user, session or request. The unit decides both the analysis and what carryover effects you are exposed to. - Primary metric and guardrails - one metric decides, a few guardrails (latency, errors, revenue) stop you shipping a win that breaks something else. - MDE and duration - the smallest effect worth acting on sets the sample size; run full weeks so weekday mix is balanced, and do not stop early because the curve looks good. Peeking without a sequential correction inflates false positives. Gotchas: novelty effects fade, so a first-week lift is not a steady-state lift; ratio metrics need a delta method or bootstrap, not a plain t-test on user ratios; and with twenty metrics something is always "significant" - pre-register the one that counts. Read the full example: related post.

docs.title: BigQuery
docs.text: Where most experiment analysis in my posts actually ran: storage separated from compute, SQL over terabytes without owning a cluster. Costs follow bytes scanned, so the gotchas are all about reading less: partition by the date you filter on, cluster by the keys you group on, select only the columns you need, and dry-run a query to see its bytes before it bills you. sql -- the dry run: shows bytes processed, runs nothing -- bq query --dry run 'SELECT ...' SELECT event name, COUNT( ) AS n FROM events WHERE event date = "2026-10-01" -- hits the partition filter GROUP BY event name SELECT on a wide events table is the classic own goal - columnar storage means you pay per column read. For repeated analysis, materialize the aggregate once and query that. Reference: BigQuery docs.

docs.title: Evaluating an agent
docs.text: A fluent answer proves nothing, so evaluate the loop rather than the vibe. Compare relevance, retrieval recall, groundedness and latency against a baseline, and read examples next to the scores: grounded, useful and found-the-right-document are three different failures. Offline golden sets give controlled comparisons; production feedback shows what the set missed, and a thumbs-down needs investigation before it means anything. My workflow produces a report for engineers rather than an automatic gate - a choice, not a rule. When a score drops, the fix depends on which failure it is: | Symptom | What it means | Where to fix | | ------- | ------------- | ------------ | | Right document, wrong answer | Groundedness | Prompt/model | | Expected source missing | Retrieval recall | Chunking, index, query | | Correct but useless | Relevance | Task framing | Always read a handful of raw examples next to any aggregate number - a metric that moved without an example you believe is a mystery, not progress. Read the full example: related post.

docs.title: Exposure triangle
docs.text: Three knobs, one budget: aperture buys light with depth of field, shutter buys it with motion blur, ISO buys it with noise, and stops are interchangeable - one more stop of ISO pays back one faster shutter. Set aperture for the look, shutter for the subject, and let ISO take the bill. One stop, three currencies: | | one stop more light | one stop less light | | --- | --- | --- | | Aperture | f/4 - f/2.8 | f/4 - f/5.6 | | Shutter | 1/250 - 1/125 | 1/250 - 1/500 | | ISO | 400 - 800 | 400 - 200 | Failure symptoms: soft edges mean the shutter was too slow, smear means subject motion, grit means the ISO was too high for the body. Same shape as tuning training: several knobs, one budget, different costs - an analogy, not a mapping.

docs.title: Forecasting
docs.text: Pick the simplest model that captures your seasonality: | Series shape | Reach for | | ------------ | --------- | | Level + trend, short history | Exponential smoothing (the baseline to beat) | | Short, well-behaved, autocorrelated | ARIMA/SARIMA | | Multiple seasonalities, holidays, gaps | Prophet - sane defaults, little tuning | Whatever the model: evaluate on rolling-origin splits, never a random split - random rows leak the future into training; a forecast is a distribution, so report intervals, not just the line; and check residuals per season, not just overall, because an annual average can hide a model that is wrong every December. Reference: Prophet.

docs.title: GAMs & LASSO
docs.text: A GAM fits one smooth curve per feature and adds them up - flexible shape, still readable effects; it was my thesis workhorse with leading indicators. LASSO pulls the other lever: keep the model linear and let the penalty push useless coefficients to zero. Reach for a GAM when the curve matters and LASSO when feature count does. | You have | You want | Pick | | -------- | -------- | ---- | | Few features, nonlinear effects | Readable curve per feature | GAM | | Many features, roughly linear effects | Automatic feature selection | LASSO | Gotchas: smoothness is a hyperparameter - too wiggly and you are fitting noise, so choose it by cross-validation, not by eye; splines extrapolate badly, so treat predictions outside the observed feature range as fiction; and standardize features before LASSO, or the penalty punishes units, not uselessness. Reference: pyGAM docs.

docs.title: Go worker pools
docs.text: A bounded worker pool separates accepting work from doing it. The queue and worker limit make overload a visible choice: wait, reject, or shed work rather than spawn without limit. The firmware comparison in the post is about keeping handlers short and defining backpressure, not treating servers like microcontrollers. The whole pattern in a few lines: go jobs := make(chan Job, 100) // bounded queue: backpressure lives here for w := 0; w < 8; w++ { // fixed workers: bounded concurrency go func() { for j := range jobs { do(j) } }() } // enqueue with select + default to shed load instead of blocking forever When the queue fills, decide explicitly: block (slow producers), reject (503 with retry-after), or shed (drop low-value work). "Unbounded" is not a fourth option; it is the first option with the bill deferred. Read the full example: related post.

docs.title: Golden datasets
docs.text: A golden set pairs questions with expected answers and source references. In the design described in the post, simulated personas propose document-anchored candidates, but people approve them before they count. Generated text is a proposal, not ground truth, and changing documents can make a once-good record stale. One record wants at least: json { "question": "How do I reset a staging deploy?", "expected answer": "...", "sources": ["runbook-deploy staging"], "approved by": "person, not the generator", "reviewed at": "2026-10-01" } Gotchas: anchor every record to a source document or you cannot detect staleness; re-review when the underlying docs change; and keep the set out of the training/prompt path - a leaked golden set measures memorization, not quality. Read the full example: related post.

docs.title: Infra as code
docs.text: Every environment change arrives as a reviewed diff, not a console click. Modules keep the repeated shape - service, database, bucket - in one place; keep them small and their variables honest, because a module with forty knobs is a second API nobody documented. The plan output is the review artifact - read it like a diff: bash terraform plan -out=tf.plan what reviewers approve terraform apply "tf.plan" exactly what was approved, nothing else Gotchas: state is the source of truth, so keep it remote, locked, and never hand-edit it; a console change made "just for now" is drift the next plan will offer to destroy; and separate state per environment, because sharing one state file is how a staging experiment becomes a production incident. Reference: Terraform modules.

docs.title: Kubeflow Pipelines
docs.text: Kubeflow Pipelines turns train-test-deploy into a DAG of containerized components on Kubernetes, each with explicit inputs and outputs. It earns its weight when pipelines are long, rerunnable and shared; a two-step nightly job is happier as a script. A component is a container plus a contract: python @component(base image="python:3.12-slim") def train(dataset: Input[Dataset], model: Output[Model], lr: float = 0.01): ... reads dataset.uri, writes model.uri Gotchas: pin the image and arguments or "reproducible" is a rumor; caching is input-based, so data that changes silently under the same inputs replays stale results - pass a data version as an explicit input when freshness matters; and keep orchestration logic out of components, because debugging Python inside YAML inside a pod is nobody's hobby. Reference: Kubeflow Pipelines docs.

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text: Kubernetes stores desired state while controllers keep trying to make the running system match it. A Deployment manages replicas, a Service gives traffic a stable destination, and Helm packages configuration. That mental model is more useful than memorising object names without knowing which controller or traffic path they belong to. The four objects that answer most questions: | Object | The question it answers | | ------ | ----------------------- | | Deployment | How many replicas, which image, how to roll | | Service | Where does traffic find the pods | | Ingress | How does outside traffic get in | | ConfigMap / Secret | Where does configuration live | Useful when something is wrong: kubectl get pods for state, kubectl describe pod for the event trail (scheduling, pulls, probes), kubectl logs --previous for the crash before the restart. Most "Kubernetes is broken" is a failing probe, a bad image tag, or resource limits - all visible in describe. Read the full example: related post.

docs.title: P95 latency
docs.text: p95 means 95% of requests were faster than this. It says nothing about the worst 5%, which is where incidents live, and the mean hides them under fast cached calls. Alert on p95 or p99, never the mean; compute from raw values or a histogram with sane buckets, never by averaging percentiles across instances; pair it with a request count so a quiet hour cannot page you. A load-test p95 is not a promise about production traffic. The Prometheus shape to remember: promql histogram quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(http request duration seconds bucket[5m]))) The sum by (le) is the part people drop - without it you average percentiles per instance, which is mathematically not a percentile. Bucket boundaries decide your resolution: a p95 can only be as precise as the buckets around it. Reference: Prometheus histogram docs. Read the full example: related post.

docs.title: MCP
docs.text: MCP is a standard socket shape between a model host and its tools: servers expose tools, resources and prompts, and any client discovers and calls them the same way. Reach for it when more than one host or team must share the same tools; one app with three functions can stay a plain function list. Gotchas: a tool's description is part of the prompt, so vague names get misused - write the description like the model reads it, with when-to-use and the argument shape; auth and what a server may see are your design, not the protocol's, so scope each server's credentials to its own data; and every tool you add competes for the model's attention, so a host with forty tools picks worse than one with five. json { "name": "search tickets", "description": "Search support tickets by keyword. Use when the user asks about past issues. Returns id, subject, status.", "input schema": { "query": "string" } } Reference: MCP introduction.

docs.title: Metric semantic layer
docs.text: A metric is more than a formula: population, event, time window and owner. Store definitions as metadata that people and programs can both read, and let a query engine compile them - the post's platform did this on BigQuery with 100+ reusable definitions. Self-service works only when the shared path is easier than writing another private SQL query; discoverability and ownership are the actual product. A definition record wants at least: yaml metric: order conversion rate population: exposed users who is in the denominator event: order completed what counts as success window: 7d attribution window after exposure owner: growth-team who answers questions about it Gotchas: changing a definition is a breaking change - version it and restate history, or dashboards silently disagree with last quarter; a metric without a named owner rots; and backfills must be reproducible, so compile from the same metadata rather than hand-editing historical numbers. Read the full example: related post.

docs.title: Multi-agent systems
docs.text: Before adding agents, ask whether the work splits into independent pieces that each need a large separate context and can run in parallel. Then a team can pay off: Anthropic's research system runs parallel subagents, beats one agent on broad queries, and costs roughly 15x the tokens. Dependent steps - clarify, retrieve, answer - are a pipeline, not a team: one agent, explicit stages, plain code between them. Chained agents in the live path are where the latency and maintenance pain shows up. The checklist before splitting: 1. Independent subtasks with separate contexts? If no, stay single-agent. 2. Parallelizable? If they must run in sequence, that is a pipeline. 3. Worth the tokens? Multiply the budget by the agent count and compare against the quality gain on an eval, not on a demo. Source: Anthropic on their multi-agent research system.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text: Instrument so a stranger can reconstruct any request after the fact: the question, what was retrieved, the answer, and the configuration in force. Dashboards show a pattern; a concrete replay tells you which component or document to fix. The three signals answer different questions: metrics say something is wrong (aggregated, cheap, alertable), traces say where (one request's path), logs say why (the detail at one point). Start an investigation from the metric, narrow with the trace, confirm in the logs. Gotchas: logs without request IDs are archaeology; record versions - model, index, config - next to every answer, or "what changed" is unanswerable; and high-cardinality labels will bankrupt the metrics bill, so keep label values to a bounded set (never user IDs or full URLs). Reference: OpenTelemetry observability primer. Read the full example: related post.

docs.title: Mixed-integer optimization
docs.text: Assign discrete resources - which truck, which delivery slot - under constraints, with a cost to minimize. I run the ops side of one in production: CVXPY to prototype the model, Kedro to keep the pipeline reproducible. Gotchas: the model is the easy half, and bad input data surfaces as infeasible at 6am - validate inputs before the solve and keep a fallback plan for solver timeouts; log the optimality gap (best bound vs incumbent), not just the objective, so "the solver stopped" has a number attached; and when a model is infeasible, ask the solver for an irreducible inconsistent subset rather than commenting out constraints one by one. python prob = cp.Problem(cp.Minimize(cost @ x), constraints) prob.solve(solver=cp.HiGHS, time limit=300) print(prob.status, prob.value) log both, every run Reference: CVXPY.

docs.title: Retrieval
docs.text: Retrieval-augmented generation finds documents, then writes an answer from them. Keep the two scores separate: recall asks whether the expected sources reached the context, groundedness asks whether the answer stayed inside them. A wrong answer with good recall is a writing problem; poor recall is a search problem, and the fixes differ. Check the expected-source set itself before trusting either number. Defaults that usually need tuning, in order of payoff: - Chunking - size and overlap decide what recall is even possible; chunks too small lose context, too large dilute the match. - Hybrid search - embeddings miss exact terms (IDs, error codes), keyword misses paraphrases; combine both and rerank. - Query rewriting - the user's words are often not the document's words. Gotcha: evaluate retrieval on its own before touching the generator, or you will tune the prompt to compensate for a bad index. Read the full example: related post.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text: Same data, same code, same result - or at least a record of why not. If you cannot diff two runs, you cannot trust the second one. The minimum kit: - Pinned dependencies - lockfiles, exact image digests; a floating tag is a time bomb. - Versioned data - a snapshot reference, not "the latest extract". - Seeded randomness - one seed recorded in the config, not scattered constants. - Config stored with output - the run's parameters next to its metrics and artifacts. "Worked on rerun" dies by a thousand unpinned cuts: a floating base-image tag, a silent data refresh, an upstream default that changed. When two runs disagree, diff the configs and the data versions first - the code is usually the third suspect. Reference: Kubeflow Pipelines caching.

docs.title: Serving SDK
docs.text: A trained model is not yet a service. The shared path should own the repeated work - authentication, tracing, deployment conventions - and stay narrow: a small ordinary path, inspectable behaviour, errors that suggest the next action. Defaults save configuration; hiding everything makes debugging impossible. When a serving change goes wrong I start at the trace and the p95, not the model. What belongs in the shared path: - Authentication and request identity, so every model gets it once. - Tracing and metrics with consistent names, wired in by default. - Versioned deploy conventions: image tag, config, model artifact recorded together. What stays out: model-specific feature logic. The test for the boundary - a data scientist should ship a model without reading platform code, and debug it without guessing what the platform hid. Read the full example: related post.

docs.title: Thompson sampling
docs.text: Reach for it when traffic is live and a fixed A/B test would keep sending users to a losing arm: sample each arm's posterior, serve the highest draw, and let uncertainty supply the exploration. In the production pattern from the post, a batch job turns repeated draws into allocation weights - request handling reads the split, it does not sample per request. The core is three lines for a binary reward: python from numpy.random import beta one posterior draw per arm; serve the argmax draw = beta(wins + 1, losses + 1) Watch out: slow rewards make new arms look worse than they are (their posterior has not caught up), reset the counts when an arm's content changes, and floor the exploration or a bad arm never quite dies. Batch updates also mean the split lags the data by one job interval - size that interval to the traffic, not to convenience. Read the full example: related post.

docs.title: Distributed traces
docs.text: A trace follows one request through every service and step it touches, turning a slow or failed call into one chain instead of unrelated log lines. Make tracing a platform default in the serving path so every model gets it for free; model-specific behaviour still needs its own checks. Gotchas: spans without consistent naming are expensive soup - settle on a convention ( service.operation , plus attributes like model.name ) and enforce it in the shared path; sample hard in volume but never sample errors; and propagate context through queues, or the chain breaks at the async boundary. On OpenTelemetry that propagation is context.inject on publish and context.extract on consume - five lines that save the whole async half of the system. Reference: OpenTelemetry traces. Read the full example: related post.

docs.title: Feedback triage
docs.text: A thumbs-down starts an investigation, not a diagnosis. The workflow replays the question, collects evidence, separates a content gap from a configuration issue, and routes to an owner; routing is ordinary code, the model only proposes the likely cause. Keep the human jobs explicit: approving a reference answer is not the same job as owning an incident, and doubtful cases go to a person rather than turning confidence into authority. The routing categories that cover most cases: - Content gap - the knowledge base does not contain the answer; route to the content owner. - Retrieval miss - the answer exists but was not found; route to search/index. - Configuration issue - wrong model, prompt or tool version in force; route to platform. - Genuine model error - everything right, answer still wrong; log for the next eval round. Read the full example: related post.

docs.title: Uplift modeling
docs.text: Model who changes behaviour because of the message, not who converts anyway. Split the audience: persuade them (target these), sure things (wasted spend), sleeping dogs (leave alone - the message backfires). Two standard approaches: - Two models - fit one model on treated, one on control, and score the difference. Simple, but each model can be good at the outcome and bad at the difference. - Transformed outcome / direct uplift learners - relabel or reweight so one model optimizes the uplift directly; usually the better default once the plumbing exists. Gotchas: you never observe the counterfactual, so evaluate with uplift or Qini curves on a held-out randomized group, not accuracy; a strong outcome model is not an uplift model; and keep a random holdout in production or you lose the yardstick you trained against. Reference: scikit-uplift docs.
